newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac's call for "new elan" spawns "elk" jokes.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's call for "new elan" spawns "elk" jokes.

text.p: Does France need a new elk?

Conservative President Jacques Chirac took a political risk when he called a parliamentary election for May 25-June 1. But he is also taking a linguistic gamble with slogans urging a "new elan" or a "shared elan" for France.
"Elan" in French means both an impulse, thrust or run-up (in sport) and an "elk", the cousin of a moose.

Serge July, publisher of the daily Liberation, said the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand rejected a similar slogan for his successful presidential campaign in 1981 on posters bearing his picture.
When his media advisors showed him a sample poster, Mitterrand drew a pair of antlers on his head and handed it back without a word.
Mitterrand went on to adopt the winning slogan "The Tranquil Force", whose only drawback was it let irreverent opponents deface "force" to "farce".

The ruling coalition's slogan for this election, "With Jacques Chirac, a shared elan" has delighted cartoonists. The satirical weekly Le Canard Enchaine depicted the two parties in the ruling centre-right as a pair of elks mating.

The opposition Socialists, hoping for an upset win, are playing it safe with the unambiguous slogan "Let's change the future", on a green background hinting at environmentalism rather than red-blooded socialism.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin appears on platforms in TV advertisements against the backdrop of a countdown of the days left until the vote: "X days to change the future".
None of the posters has captured the imagination as Chirac did by successfully exploiting the apple tree as a symbol of growth and renewal in his drive for the presidency in 1995.

His winning slogan, beside a tree sprouting red apples, was "France for All". He now says that France needs a "new elan" to tackle problems such as record unemployment and prepare for a single European currency.
The coalition's posters proclaiming a "shared elan" show three hands reaching out into a clear blue sky -- apparently representing a man, a woman and a child.
There is no head to which antlers could be added.

The television satire show Les Guignols de l'Info (the news clowns) portrayed the hands as those of three people drowning. Other wags suggested they stood for the hands of the poor outstretched to beg.

Some have joked the posters may undermine the traditionally right-wing Catholic vote in France -- neither the man nor the woman have a wedding ring. And the hands are without calluses, perhaps jeopardising the manual workers' vote.
Campaign officials at the RPR-UDF coalition say hundreds of thousands have been printed although few seem to have made their way on to billboards so far.
French campaigns are littered with failed slogans.
Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing miscalculated in 1981 when he tried to play on his experience against the untested Mitterrand with the slogan: "France needs a president".
It flopped because voters took it as a painful statement of the obvious -- yes, that's what elections are for.

Giscard's ambitions also came unstuck because opponents glued cut-out diamonds to his eyes on his posters. He was under fire for having accepted a gift of diamonds from late Central African dictator Jean-Bedel Bokassa.
